results.corrected_claim: The quoted Apple text is real. ControlSize.extraLarge is declared as `case extraLarge` and is available on iOS 17.0, iPadOS 17.0, Mac Catalyst 17.0, macOS 14.0, tvOS 17.0, visionOS 1.0 and watchOS 10.0. None of these is beta or deprecated. Its abstract says, verbatim: "A control version that is substantially sized. The largest control size. Resolves to large on platforms other than visionOS." The conclusion drawn from it is not established, though: that iOS never renders a distinct extra-large size and that the skill's padding token is therefore meaningless. That abstract dates from the iOS 17 / macOS 14 era, and newer Apple sources contradict it in part. The Adopting Liquid Glass overview says "Controls also feature an option for an extra-large size, allowing more space for labels and accents." The iOS & iPadOS 26 release notes (SwiftUI, 144417732) say "In iOS and iPadOS apps that adopt the new design, a picker of .segmented style now supports .large and .extraLarge control sizes." WWDC25-323 says "And for your most important, prominent actions there is now support for extra large sized buttons." AppKit also added NSControl.ControlSize.extraLarge in macOS 26.0, which contradicts the abstract for macOS. No primary source says whether a Button with .extraLarge renders larger than .large on iOS 26 or 27. One more point: 01-api-reference.md:268 calls .extraLarge "new in iOS 26", but it has been available since iOS 17.0.
results.notes: Primary sources, all fetched as DocC JSON: swiftui/controlsize/extralarge.json and swiftui/controlsize.json (verbatim abstract and availability); appkit/nscontrol/controlsize-swift.enum/extralarge.json (macOS 26.0, so the abstract is stale for macOS); ios-ipados-26-release-notes.json, SwiftUI > New Features, 144417732 (segmented picker supports .extraLarge on iOS); technologyoverviews/adopting-liquid-glass.json, Controls section; WWDC25 323 transcript (Controls chapter, mostly macOS context); WWDC25 356 ("the new X-Large size", macOS context). Forum thread 740326 (2023, Apple Frameworks Engineer) shows the "maps .extraLarge to .large" behaviour predates macOS 26. The HIG Buttons page lists Extra large (64 pt) for visionOS only and gives no iOS size table. UIButton.Configuration.Size has no extraLarge (large, medium, small, mini). The June 2026 and September 2026 SwiftUI updates and the iOS 27 release notes do not mention extraLarge. The skill's padding tokens (28/18) are the skill's own invention and do not come from Apple. Verdict: the doc quote is accurate, but the behavioural claim for iOS buttons is unverified and possibly stale.

results.corrected_claim: `.controlSize(.extraLarge)` appears at examples/03-OnboardingFlow.swift:75 and examples/08-LoginScreen.swift:367. It compiles on iOS 17.0+ (not deprecated). Apple's ControlSize reference says it "Resolves to large on platforms other than visionOS", so in the worst case the CTA renders the same as .large and nothing breaks. Apple's 26-era sources describe an extra-large control size as part of the new design: Adopting Liquid Glass ("Controls also feature an option for an extra-large size"), WWDC25-323 ("support for extra large sized buttons"), and the iOS 26 release notes for segmented pickers on iOS. No primary source confirms either way whether iOS renders Buttons at .extraLarge any larger than .large. The finding's statement that iOS "does not render" a larger size is therefore not established. It holds only if the reference abstract is current for iOS Buttons, which cannot be confirmed without a device or newer docs.
results.notes: Same evidence as finding 20. The usages were confirmed in the repo at the cited lines, plus 01-api-reference.md:268 and :283, and 03-design-tokens.md:40 and :154. Conflicting primary sources: the ControlSize.extraLarge abstract (stale for macOS, since AppKit gained extraLarge in macOS 26.0) against the iOS & iPadOS 26 release notes, SwiftUI 144417732 ("In iOS and iPadOS apps that adopt the new design, a picker of .segmented style now supports .large and .extraLarge control sizes."). These examples are at most a documentation-accuracy issue, not a functional bug.

results.corrected_claim: Apple describes the Liquid Glass look as a Settings preference separate from the accessibility settings. Adopting Liquid Glass says: "people can choose a preferred look for Liquid Glass in their device's settings, or turn on accessibility settings that reduce transparency or motion in the interface... If you use standard components from system frameworks, this experience adapts automatically. Ensure you test your app's custom elements, colors, and animations with different configurations of these settings." HIG Materials says the variants' "appearance... can differ in response to certain system settings, like if people choose a preferred look for Liquid Glass in their device's settings, or turn on accessibility settings that reduce transparency or increase contrast". In the 27 releases, WWDC26-102 (Platforms State of the Union) says: "a new slider in settings to adjust Liquid Glass anywhere from ultra clear to fully tinted". WWDC26-269 (What's new in SwiftUI) says: "Liquid Glass has a refined look and automatically responds to the new Liquid Glass slider to adjust its tint." The iOS 26.1 details come only from secondary sources: a Clear/Tinted choice at Settings > Display & Brightness > Liquid Glass. That contradicts the skill's path, Settings > Accessibility > Display. SwiftUI exposes no API that reads this preference.
results.notes: Quotes verified verbatim from: the WWDC26 102 and 269 transcripts; design/human-interface-guidelines/materials.json; technologyoverviews/adopting-liquid-glass.json. No public API: swiftui/environmentvalues.json (both halves read) has only accessibilityReduceTransparency, colorSchemeContrast, backgroundMaterial and materialActiveAppearance as related members. swiftui/glass.json has only clear, identity, regular, interactive(_:) and tint(_:), with no 27.0 additions. The iOS 26.1 and iOS 27 developer release notes do not mention the setting. The 26.1 Clear/Tinted location could not be confirmed from a primary source, because support.apple.com and apple.com were unreachable; it is corroborated only by secondary sources (Tom's Guide, Macworld, Notebookcheck). The finding itself labels that part secondary. The skill is right that system and standard glass adapts automatically. It is wrong to file this under Accessibility, to describe it as an "opacity multiplier", and to treat it as a 26.1-only binary mode now that it is a slider in the 27 releases.

results.corrected_claim: HIG Materials says, verbatim: "Don't use Liquid Glass in the content layer. ... Instead, use standard materials for elements in the content layer, such as app backgrounds." Its iOS/iPadOS section adds: "In addition to Liquid Glass, iOS and iPadOS continue to provide four standard materials — ultra-thin, thin, regular (default), and thick — which you can use in the content layer to help create visual distinction." SwiftUI Material (iOS 15.0+) and Material.ultraThin are not deprecated on any platform. The skill's blanket ban on .ultraThinMaterial and other "legacy" Material values in iOS 26+ therefore contradicts Apple's guidance. The ban appears at SKILL.md:88 and :12, 02-hig-principles.md:162 and pre-ship-checklist.md:9. The correct rule: use Liquid Glass for the controls and navigation layer, and use standard materials (not glass) for content-layer surfaces. Adopting Liquid Glass separately advises "Reduce your use of custom backgrounds in controls and navigation elements."
results.notes: Verified via design/human-interface-guidelines/materials.json (change log latest: September 9, 2025, "Updated guidance for Liquid Glass"), swiftui/material.json (iOS 15.0+, deprecated false on every platform), swiftui/material/ultrathin.json (iOS 15.0+, not deprecated) and technologyoverviews/adopting-liquid-glass.json. The skill's golden rule 1 (no glass on content backgrounds) agrees with HIG; only the material ban and the "legacy" label are wrong.

results.corrected_claim: All of the finding's Apple quotes check out verbatim against "Applying Liquid Glass to custom views". The article says: "The larger the spacing value on the container, the sooner the Liquid Glass effects behind views blend together and merge the shapes during a transition. A spacing value on the container that's larger than the spacing of an interior HStack, VStack, or other layout container causes Liquid Glass effects to blend together at rest because the views are too close to each other." It also says "Creating too many Liquid Glass effect containers and applying too many effects to views outside of containers can degrade performance." The GlassEffectContainer overview says: "As shapes near one another, their paths start to blend into one another. The higher the spacing, the sooner blending begins as the shapes approach each other." The declaration also checks out: `@MainActor @preconcurrency init(spacing: CGFloat? = nil, @ContentBuilder content: () -> Content)`. It is the only initializer listed. It is available on iOS, iPadOS, Mac Catalyst, macOS, tvOS and watchOS 26.0; visionOS is not listed. The skill's line 122 is not wrong about direction: "Larger values = elements merge from further away" matches Apple, and Apple's example morphs when the nearest edge is less than or equal to the container's spacing. It is incomplete, because it implies blending happens only during transitions. Apple says that when container spacing exceeds the inner stack spacing, shapes blend even at rest. So GlassEffectContainer(spacing: 80) at 04-motion:118 will fuse siblings at rest if they sit closer than 80 pt. A real error the finding did not cite is at 04-motion:116: "spacing: 8 // morph aggressively" reverses Apple's rule, since a smaller spacing means later, less blending. The skill's signature block also shows @ViewBuilder and a separate init without spacing; current docs show a single init(spacing:content:) with `= nil` and @ContentBuilder.
results.notes: Fetched: swiftui/applying-liquid-glass-to-custom-views.json (full article quoted), swiftui/glasseffectcontainer.json (overview and availability) and swiftui/glasseffectcontainer/init(spacing:content:).json (declaration tokens). Calling the skill's line "factually-wrong" overstates it: it is incomplete or misleading, not inverted. The quoted performance sentence is relevant mainly to the skill's claim that a container is "Required whenever two or more glass elements live near each other".

results.corrected_claim: Verbatim declarations: `nonisolated func glassEffectID(_ id: (some Hashable & Sendable)?, in namespace: Namespace.ID) -> some View` and `@MainActor @preconcurrency func glassEffectUnion(id: (some Hashable & Sendable)?, namespace: Namespace.ID) -> some View`. Both are available on iOS 26.0, iPadOS 26.0, Mac Catalyst 26.0, macOS 26.0, tvOS 26.0 and watchOS 26.0; visionOS is not listed, and neither is beta or deprecated. The skill's `<ID: Hashable>(_ id: ID ...)` and `<ID: Hashable>(id: ID ...)` signatures are wrong: the ID must also be Sendable and is Optional. The labels (_:in:) and (id:namespace:) are correct. Union semantics from the doc: "All Liquid Glass effects with the same shape and Liquid Glass variant will be combined into a single shape." From the article: "This combines all effects with a similar shape, Liquid Glass effect, and ID into a single shape with the applied Liquid Glass material." The skill's description, "Forces two non-adjacent glass views to render as a single unified glass shape", leaves out the same-shape and same-variant requirement.
results.notes: Fetched swiftui/view/glasseffectid(_:in:).json and swiftui/view/glasseffectunion(id:namespace:).json (declaration tokens, availability, discussion), plus the Applying Liquid Glass article. Caveat: Apple's docs do not say what passing nil does. "Optional allows passing nil to conditionally drop the ID or union" is a reasonable inference from the type, not documented behaviour. A bare `nil` literal also cannot infer the opaque type; it needs a typed optional. String and Int literal IDs used in the skill are Sendable, so its examples still compile. Only custom non-Sendable ID types would fail.
